headline: Two More Newspapers Sue AI Companies Over Using Their News Stories

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Two newspapers, The Seattle Times and Newsday, are unhappy with a company called OpenAI and another company called Microsoft. OpenAI makes a computer program called ChatGPT that can chat with people and write things. Microsoft makes a similar program called CoPilot. These programs learn by reading huge amounts of writing, including news stories. The newspapers say the companies used their stories to teach these programs without asking permission or paying for it. Because of this, the newspapers are taking the companies to court, which is called a lawsuit. They worry that if AI programs keep copying news stories, people might stop needing real newspapers at all, and that could hurt the reporters who work hard to find and write true stories. This is not the first time this has happened. Last year, a big newspaper called The New York Times did the same thing. A person from Microsoft said the company was surprised by the lawsuit but is willing to talk about it and try to fix the problem.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Two news organizations, The Seattle Times and Newsday, have filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft. These companies created popular AI tools like ChatGPT and CoPilot, which can answer questions and write text almost like a person. To learn how to do this, AI programs are trained on huge amounts of text from the internet, including news articles. The newspapers claim their stories were used to train these AI tools without permission or payment. They argue this is unfair because the AI then creates content that competes with the very newspapers it learned from. The lawsuit describes this as dangerous for the news industry, since fewer people might read original news stories if AI can summarize or recreate them for free. This case is part of a bigger pattern. In 2023, The New York Times filed a similar lawsuit against the same companies, and several other publications have joined in since then. What makes this new lawsuit interesting is that Microsoft and OpenAI have actually given money to The Seattle Times in the past to support journalism projects and training programs for reporters. This makes the disagreement more complicated because the two sides have worked together before. Microsoft responded by saying it was surprised by the lawsuit, but said it is open to sitting down and talking about how to solve the problem instead of only fighting in court. This story matters because it could affect how news is shared, protected, and paid for in the future, especially as AI technology keeps growing more powerful.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: The Seattle Times and Newsday have become the latest news organizations to sue OpenAI and Microsoft, accusing the companies of using their journalism without permission to train artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT and CoPilot. These AI programs work by analyzing massive amounts of existing text, including news articles, to learn how to generate humanlike writing. The newspapers argue that this process amounts to stealing their work, since the AI tools can then produce summaries or content that resemble the original articles without paying the journalists or publications that created them. The lawsuit uses a striking metaphor, comparing generative AI to a snake eating its own tail, suggesting that AI could eventually destroy the very news organizations it depends on for information. The papers argue that AI companies present themselves as creators of new content, when really they are copying and repackaging work made by real journalists. This case adds to a growing trend of legal battles between news organizations and AI companies. The New York Times filed a similar lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft back in 2023, arguing copyright infringement, and other publishers have since joined the fight. What makes the Seattle Times lawsuit especially notable is that Microsoft and OpenAI previously funded some of the newspaper's journalism initiatives and training fellowships, meaning the two sides had a working relationship before this legal dispute began. This raises questions about how technology companies and news organizations should treat each other, since they may need to cooperate for funding and technology, while also competing over how content gets used. In response, a Microsoft spokesperson said the company was surprised by the lawsuit but remains willing to discuss possible solutions rather than only fight it out in court. This story is important because it touches on bigger questions about fairness, ownership, and money in the age of artificial intelligence. If courts decide that AI companies must pay for using copyrighted material, it could change how AI tools are built in the future. If not, some worry that quality journalism could become harder to fund, since fewer readers might visit original news websites when AI can summarize the information instead.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: The Seattle Times and Newsday have joined a growing list of news organizations suing OpenAI and Microsoft, alleging that the companies used their journalism without authorization or compensation to train generative AI systems like ChatGPT and CoPilot. These AI tools function by processing enormous datasets of text, including online news articles, so they can learn to generate humanlike responses and written content. The lawsuit claims this amounts to unauthorized use of copyrighted material, arguing that AI companies benefit financially from content they did not create while providing little to no compensation to the original authors and publishers. The complaint uses vivid language, describing generative AI as “a snake eating its own tail,” implying that AI could ultimately undermine and destroy the news industry it depends upon for training material. The lawsuit further asserts that AI products are marketed as tools that produce original content, when in reality they consume human-created journalism and generate derivative versions of it, sometimes competing directly with the sources they were trained on. This legal action follows a similar, high-profile lawsuit filed by The New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, which argued copyright infringement over the use of Times articles in AI training data. Since then, several other publishers have filed comparable lawsuits, signaling a broader industry-wide concern about how AI companies are using journalistic content. What sets the Seattle Times case apart is the underlying relationship between the parties. Microsoft and OpenAI have previously provided funding for some of the newspaper's journalism projects and professional fellowships, meaning the companies had already collaborated with the publication before this dispute emerged. This complicates the narrative, showing that even organizations receiving support from tech companies may still pursue legal action if they believe their intellectual property rights are being violated. In response to the lawsuit, a Microsoft spokesperson stated the company was surprised by the legal action but expressed a willingness to discuss potential resolutions outside of court. This ongoing conflict raises significant questions about intellectual property law in the age of artificial intelligence, including how existing copyright frameworks apply to AI training, whether news organizations deserve compensation when their work fuels AI development, and how these legal decisions might shape the future relationship between the technology and journalism industries. The outcome of these lawsuits could influence how AI companies license content going forward, potentially reshaping the economics of journalism and the accessibility of AI tools alike.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: The Seattle Times and Newsday have become the latest news organizations to file a lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft, alleging that the companies used their copyrighted journalism without permission or compensation to train generative AI systems such as ChatGPT and CoPilot. These AI models are built by processing vast quantities of text data, including news articles scraped from the internet, in order to learn patterns of language and generate humanlike responses. The lawsuit contends that this practice constitutes copyright infringement, since the AI companies allegedly profit commercially from content they did not produce, while offering little or no compensation to the journalists and organizations whose work formed the foundation of that training data. The complaint employs pointed rhetorical language, describing generative AI as “a snake eating its own tail,” a metaphor suggesting that AI's reliance on journalistic content could ultimately erode or destroy the very news industry that supplies its raw material. The lawsuit further argues that AI products are marketed to the public as original content generators, when in fact they function as derivative systems, ingesting human-authored journalism and reproducing imitative versions of it, sometimes directly competing with the original sources in the marketplace for information and advertising revenue. This legal action is part of a broader wave of litigation that began in 2023, when The New York Times filed a prominent lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft over similar copyright infringement claims. Since then, numerous other publishers have filed comparable suits, reflecting mounting concern across the journalism industry about how AI companies acquire and use copyrighted material without clear licensing agreements or consistent legal precedent. A particularly noteworthy aspect of the Seattle Times case is the prior financial relationship between the parties: Microsoft and OpenAI had previously funded several of the newspaper's journalism initiatives and professional fellowship programs. This detail complicates the dispute, illustrating that even organizations that have benefited from technology industry partnerships and funding may still pursue legal remedies when they believe their intellectual property rights are being infringed upon. In response to the lawsuit, a Microsoft spokesperson stated that the company was surprised by the legal action but remained open to discussing potential solutions outside of formal litigation, signaling a preference for negotiated resolution over prolonged court battles. This unfolding legal conflict raises substantive questions about how existing copyright law, largely developed before the emergence of generative AI, should apply to machine learning systems trained on copyrighted material. It also highlights tension between the technology sector's drive toward AI innovation and the journalism industry's need for sustainable revenue models. The resolution of these cases could set important legal precedents affecting how AI companies license content moving forward, potentially reshaping the financial viability of journalism, the future development of AI technology, and the broader relationship between content creators and the platforms that rely on their work.

questions: If AI tools can summarize news for free, how might that change the way you and your family get information about the world?
Do you think it's fair for companies to use news articles to train AI without paying the people who wrote them? Why or why not?
How might this lawsuit affect local newspapers or reporters in your own community in the future?
